Blamelessness
BLAYM-les-nes
n.
From blameless + -ness. Renders the Greek amemptos, “blameless, faultless,” and amōmos, “without spot or blemish”; and the Hebrew tāmīm, “complete, sound, blameless.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Blamelessness in Scripture is not sinless perfection—Scripture never claims that for any but Christ—but the practical, walk-and-conduct standing of a believer against whom no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained. The Hebrew tāmīm is the great Old Testament word: Noah was perfect (tāmīm) in his generations; Abraham was charged, walk before me, and be thou perfect; Job was perfect and upright; the priestly sacrifices were to be without blemish—the same word applied morally to persons. The Greek amemptos means literally “not to be blamed”: Paul commends the Philippians to be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation; Zacharias and Elisabeth were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless; Paul says of himself touching the righteousness which is in the law, he was blameless. The qualifications for elders and deacons in the Pastorals turn on this very category: a bishop then must be blameless; let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless. Blamelessness is therefore a real, achievable, expected standing of every mature believer and especially every officer of the church—not perfection, but the absence of any legitimate moral or doctrinal charge that can be sustained against him by a fair examination. It includes the open, walking-in-the-light life that has nothing to hide; the long, consistent pattern of conduct that gives no occasion for credible accusation; the integrity that aligns the inward and outward man; and the readiness, when accusation is made falsely, to bear it with the calm conscience of one who knows that the charge is not true. The eschatological promise gathers the doctrine to its consummation: that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish—the church Christ will at last present to Himself in the perfect blamelessness toward which the saint’s present sanctification is being shaped, by the Spirit, in his own life now.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BLAMELESS as without fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure; in scripture, the practical walk and conduct against which no legitimate charge can be sustained.

expand to see more

BLAMELESS, a. — Without fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure. A bishop then must be blameless (1 Tim 3:2). 2. Free from imputation of fault; harmless; unblamable; as, to live a blameless life.

BLAMELESSNESS, n. — Innocence; a state of being not deserving of censure; the practical walk and conduct of one against whom no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained.

📖 Key Scripture

Philippians 2:15 — "That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world."

1 Timothy 3:2 — "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach."

Luke 1:6 — "And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless."

Ephesians 5:27 — "That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Blamelessness is corrupted, on one side, by the perfectionist register that treats it as sinless perfection unattainable in this life and so quietly drops the standard altogether—and on the other by the laxist register that has so lowered the bar for officers and members that the New Testament’s blameless qualifications are no longer practically applied.

expand to see more

The perfectionist corruption confuses blamelessness with sinless perfection and so concludes that the standard cannot be met in this life and need not be pressed in pastoral practice. Scripture refuses the confusion. Zacharias and Elisabeth were blameless, yet Zacharias was struck dumb for unbelief moments after his blamelessness was named—the category is real, the perfection is not yet. Paul names himself blameless touching the law’s righteousness and elsewhere counts that righteousness as dung. The two stand together. Blamelessness is the practical walk-and-conduct standing of one against whom no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained; it is real, achievable, and expected of mature believers and especially of officers; it is not sinless perfection, which awaits the resurrection. Recover the distinction, and the standard returns to its proper pastoral use: not as an impossible counsel of perfection but as the real, examinable walk Scripture commands and the church is to require of those it sets in office.

The opposite and more contemporary corruption is the laxist register that has so lowered the bar for officers and members that the New Testament’s blameless qualifications are no longer practically applied. Elders are ordained whose lives are known to bear credible moral charges; deacons are appointed without serious examination; the very category of a scandalous Christian—one whose life gives such occasion for credible accusation that his name itself is a stumbling-block to the gospel—is treated indulgently rather than addressed. Scripture is sharper. A bishop then must be blameless—the requirement is given because the office requires it, because the church’s credibility before the watching world depends in part upon it, and because the saint’s own walk is built up or torn down by the patterns of conduct his shepherds embody. Recover the standard. Examine those proposed for office, address scandalous patterns through the discipline Scripture appoints, and aim the whole body toward the blamelessness Paul commands as the practical fruit of the gospel: blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek amemptos (not to be blamed) and amōmos (without spot or blemish); Hebrew tāmīm (complete, sound, blameless)—the practical walk-and-conduct standing against which no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained.

expand to see more

Greek amemptos (G273) — blameless, faultless (Phil 2:15; Luke 1:6; 1 Thess 3:13).

Greek amōmos (G299) — without spot or blemish (Eph 1:4; 5:27; Heb 9:14; Jude 24).

Greek anepilemptos (G423) — not to be laid hold of, irreproachable (1 Tim 3:2 of bishops).

Hebrew tāmīm (H8549) — complete, sound, blameless (Gen 6:9; 17:1; Job 1:1; Ps 15:2).

Usage

"Blamelessness is not sinless perfection but the practical walk against which no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained."

"A bishop then must be blameless—the requirement is given because the office requires it and the church’s credibility depends in part upon it."

"Perfectionist confusion drops the standard as unattainable; laxist confusion drops it as inconvenient; biblical blamelessness is real, examinable, and expected of mature believers."
